paras: The peonage arrests of the Young brothers took place in Lafayette County, Mississippi, on August 24, 1905, when federal officers arrested Brigham, Allen and James Young, Lee Rogers and Charles Butts, five white men, on a charge of holding John Ross, a Black man, in bondage. The five gave bond to appear before a United States commissioner on September 5. The local Oxford Eagle called it the first peonage arrest in the county, and the case ran as a short dispatch in papers from New York to Texas.

The Youngs were described as well-to-do people who owned a large farm and a sawmill in the southwestern part of the county, near where they were arrested. A Memphis telegram to the New-York Tribune described three of the accused as wealthy brothers who owned plantations as well as the mill.

According to the charge, the five men held Ross "in bondage and otherwise restrained him of his liberty." The Memphis telegram added that the brothers worked him at the mill and on their farms and, "it is said," turned him over to the other two men when they needed him. The same report stated that the men were alleged to have said they were holding and working him for debts owed to all five.
Deputy United States marshals made the arrests on Thursday, August 24, in the southwestern part of Lafayette County.

All five gave bond for their appearance before United States Commissioner Lem E. Oldham on Tuesday, September 5. No report of that hearing, an indictment or a trial appears in the coverage, and no statement from Ross or the accused was printed.

Only white papers carried the case, in brief news items without editorial comment. The New-York Tribune put it on its front page on August 26 under the headline "Arrested for Peonage. Five Planters Charged with Offence Against One Negro," naming neither the accused nor Ross and hedging its details with "it is said" and "it is alleged." An Oxford dispatch naming all six men ran the same day in the Louisville Courier-Journal, and a fuller special appeared in the San Antonio Daily Light on August 27.

Within Mississippi, the Port Gibson Reveille reprinted the Oxford item among its state news on August 31. The same day the Oxford Eagle gave the arrest a single paragraph among local notes on quarantine and visitors, noting only that it was the county's first peonage case. No coverage of the case was found in the Black press.
The San Antonio special placed the arrests in the southwestern part of "this city," while the Oxford Eagle and the Port Gibson reprint of the same item said the county, which is the likelier reading.

reader.title: Peonage arrests of the Young brothers in Lafayette County, Mississippi
bases: Five white men were arrested by federal officers on a charge of peonage for holding John Ross, a Black man, in bondage and working him to pay claimed debts (A1, A2, A5).

The local Oxford Eagle and separate Oxford and Memphis dispatches agree on the five arrests and the peonage charge involving one Black man (A1, A2, A5); the underlying holding of Ross is reported only as the federal charge.

accounts.label: Federal charge (Oxford dispatches and local paper)
accounts.gist: Deputy U.S. marshals arrested five white men charged with holding John Ross, a negro, in bondage and restraining his liberty; they gave bond for a hearing.

accounts.label: Memphis telegram
accounts.gist: Three wealthy planter brothers and two others 'seem' to have worked one unnamed negro by turns at their mill and farms, reportedly saying they held him for debts due all five.

framing.detail: The Tribune ran 'Arrested for Peonage. Five Planters Charged with Offence Against One Negro' on page 1 as a short telegram, hedging the facts as 'it is said' and 'it is alleged'.
The Oxford Eagle placed the arrest among local items as 'the first arrest in LaFayette County on the charge of peonage', without comment.
The Courier-Journal, San Antonio Daily Light and Port Gibson Reveille carried brief Oxford dispatches attributing the bondage claim with 'it is claimed'.

conflicts.note: The local Eagle places the arrests in the county; the San Antonio text's 'city' is likely an error, as its own reprint in the Port Gibson Reveille reads 'county'.

versions.value: Dispatch dated Aug. 25 reporting the arrests

conflicts.note: The datelines give only the date of filing; the local weekly's 'last Thursday' fixes Aug. 24.

record_check.dossier: Arrests were in the southwestern part of Lafayette County; Oxford is the dateline and seat of the U.S. commissioner, not the place of the events
Brigham, Allen and James Young, Lee Rogers and Charles Butts, white planters
held in bondage, restrained of liberty, worked by turns at mill and farms (as charged)

record_check.record: working him by turns ... for debts they said he owed all five
record_check.dossier: Supported, but the working by turns and the debt claim come from one Memphis telegram and are hedged as 'it is said'/'it is alleged'

info: Arrests made Thursday, Aug. 24, 1905 ('last Thursday' in the Aug. 31 local weekly); wire datelines Aug. 25-26
Southwestern part of Lafayette County, near the Youngs' farm and sawmill
John Ross, a Black man ('a negro')
None against Ross; the accused said they held him for debts due all five
Brigham Young, Allen Young, James Young, Lee Rogers and Charles Butts, white; three described as wealthy brothers owning a sawmill and plantations
No report of the Sept. 5 hearing, an indictment or a trial was found
